faq: What is the difference between a role and a permission?
A permission is a single allowed action, like deleting a project. A role is a named bundle of permissions, like admin. People get roles, so one change updates many rules.
Can I use a library or service for this?
Yes. Tools like Casbin, CASL or your auth provider's roles can help. We pick what fits your stack, and explain the choice so your developers are comfortable with it.
Can you add roles to an app that has none?
Yes. We start by giving every current user a sensible default role, so nothing breaks, then add the new rules step by step and test each one.
How do I know nothing is missed?
We list every action and screen, test each role against the list and share the results. No one can promise zero gaps, but a written check makes the gaps visible.

desc:
Role-based access control for SaaS products decides who can see and do what, and enforces it on every request. Ecom Swift LLC defines your roles with you, then builds and tests the permission checks in your own app.

## What is role-based access control?

Role-based access control, often shortened to RBAC, assigns people to roles and gives each role a set of permissions. A permission is one allowed action, such as "invite a member" or "delete a project". A role is a named bundle of permissions, such as owner, admin, editor or viewer.

The idea is simple: you decide the rules once, in one place, and each user inherits them through their role.

## Why access rules matter once you have more than one kind of user

Early products often treat everyone the same. That works until a customer asks whether a new hire can read reports without changing billing. If the answer is no, your product has a gap that no amount of trust can close.

The usual failures are quiet ones. A button is hidden in the interface, but the underlying request still works, so anyone who knows the address can use it. Or checks are scattered across the code, and a new feature ships without any. Both leave data open to the wrong person.

## How clear permissions affect sales and trust

Business buyers look for access rules before they commit. A manager needs to give an intern limited access and a partner read-only access. Without roles, they cannot adopt your product widely, so they keep it with one person.

Roles also reduce accidents. A viewer cannot delete the project, and an editor cannot change billing. They work because mistakes are limited by design, not by good intentions. For you, the benefit is fewer support cases that start with "someone deleted our data" and an easier answer to security questionnaires.

## What a great permission system includes

- A written list of roles and what each one can do.
- A permission table everyone on your team can read.
- Checks on the server for every protected action, not only in the interface.
- Features and menu items hidden or disabled to match the role.
- A screen where an owner can change a member's role.
- A safe rule that a team always keeps at least one owner.
- Clear messages when someone lacks permission.
- Tests covering each role against each protected action.
- Optional custom roles that customers define for themselves.
- A log of permission changes showing who changed what.

## What we do

We start with a workshop-style conversation to list your actions and the kinds of people who use them. From that we draft the roles and the permission table, and you approve it before any code is written.

Then we build the checks. A central rule set answers the question "may this user do this?", and every protected route and action asks it. We apply the same rules to the interface so people see only what they can use. After that we test each role against each action and give you a report of what passed.

The Basic package covers three fixed roles and checks on up to ten actions. Standard supports up to five roles, up to twenty-five actions, server blocking, a role-setting screen and a test report. Premium covers up to eight roles plus customer-defined custom roles, up to fifty actions, and a log of permission changes, with a handover call.

## What to do and what to avoid

**Do:**
- Give each role the fewest permissions it needs.
- Enforce access rules on the back end with each call, not only in the interface.
- Name roles after jobs people recognize.
- Keep at least one owner on every account.
- Record changes to roles and permissions.

**Avoid:**
- Hiding a button and calling the feature protected.
- Creating a new role for every one-off request.
- Mixing role names with plan names.
- Allowing users to raise their own role.
- Adding features without deciding which role may use them.

## Who this is for

It suits a SaaS product whose first business customers are asking for admin and member levels. It also fits a team whose app has a single "is admin" flag and needs finer control. An agency portal that gives clients limited views of shared work is another good case.

## What we need from you

Send a list of the main screens and actions, plus any rules customers have already asked for. We need collaborator or developer access to the project and a test environment, and we will ask for a few test users. We never need passwords. If you use an outside login or access service, tell us so we fit the rules to it.
